summaryTr: Revised Criminal Procedure Law passes National Assembly, only presidential ratification remains

editorial.titleTr: Opinion: A Nation Where Drug-Intoxicated Women in Their 20s Crawl on All Fours Through the Streets
summaryTr: A woman in her 20s was found crawling on all fours under the influence of drugs at Suwon Station.
Drug-related offenses have surged since 2021, exceeding 20,000 cases for three consecutive years starting in 2023.
With prosecutors' investigative authority curtailed, drug enforcement capabilities have weakened, raising concerns that South Korea could become a haven for drugs.
editorial.bodyTr:
A woman who engaged in bizarre behavior—jumping in place and crawling on all fours—near Suwon Station during rush hour last month was booked by police on drug charges, according to the Suwon Paldal Police Station.

Around 9:20 a.m. on the 29th of last month, near Suwon Station in Gyeonggi Province, a woman who was screaming, jumping in place, and crawling on all fours on the pavement was booked by police on suspicion of drug use. According to the Suwon Paldal Police Station, the woman tested positive for methamphetamine in a preliminary drug test and admitted to using the substance. The Suwon Station drug incident, in which a woman crawled on all fours like a "zombie" through the streets during weekday commute hours, cannot be dismissed as merely an individual's lapse in judgment. It should be seen as symbolic of how drugs have insidiously infiltrated Korean society like poisonous mushrooms, destroying the lives and health of citizens.

The severity of the problem lies in the fact that similar incidents continue to occur. In February, a woman in her 30s drove a sports car while intoxicated on propofol, a medical anesthetic, and crashed through the railing of Seoul's Banpo Bridge into a riverside park. How is this different from drug-ravaged America, tainted by Chinese-made fentanyl?

Drug-related offenses have surged since 2021. In 2023, the number first exceeded 20,000, and it has remained above that threshold for three consecutive years. According to the National Investigation Service of the Police Agency, 5,203 drug offenders were arrested during intensive crackdowns from March to June, with 1,039 being detained. Of the arrested drug offenders, approximately four out of every ten distributed or purchased drugs through online non-face-to-face transactions via SNS and other platforms. Drugs now spare no one—housewives and teenagers alike are affected.

South Korea had long been a "drug-free nation." Since 1989, it established a dedicated narcotics division at the Supreme Prosecutors' Office and systematically investigated and cracked down on drug offenses. However, in 2020, the Moon Jae-in administration scaled back the prosecution's dedicated drug investigation unit and limited the scope of direct prosecution investigations to certain drug supply crimes, citing adjustment of investigative authority between prosecutors and police. This significantly weakened drug investigations.

The Police Agency began intensive drug crackdowns starting this month through December. However, with the Democratic Party's push to completely abolish the prosecution's supplementary investigative authority, prosecutors will withdraw from drug investigations starting next October. It is doubtful whether the police alone possess the capacity to properly conduct drug investigations that require international cooperation. With drug addiction and drug crimes on the rise while investigative capacity actually shrinks, it is impossible not to worry that South Korea could become a breeding ground for drugs.

editorial.title: Demographic threshold
editorial.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population. 한국이 하루아침에 늙은 사회가 된 것은 아니다. 하지만 모든 사회는 결국 인구통계 예측이 미래를 설명하는 것에서 현재를 설명하는 것으로 바뀌는 시점에 도달한다. 그 순간이 이번 주에 찾아왔다. 통계청이 지난 화요일 발표한 2025년 공식 인구조사 데이터에 따르면 65세 이상 인구가 전체 인구의 20.7%를 차지하면서 한국이 공식적으로 세계 초고령 사회 대열에 합류했다. 동시에 경제활동 가능 인구는 69.2%로 하락해 2015년 이후 비교 가능한 통계가 시작된 이래 처음으로 70% 아래로 내려갔다. 이 수치들은 임의적 기준을 넘어섰다는 점보다는 더욱 중요한 현실을 확인시켜준다는 점에서 의미가 있다. 한국은 더 이상 인구 구조 변화를 앞두고 있는 것이 아니라 이미 그것을 완성한 상태다. 따라서 이제 문제는 인구 구조를 어떻게 회복할 것인가가 아니라 생산성과 사회적 응집력을 훼손하지 않으면서 영구적으로 고령화되고 성장 속도가 느려진 사회를 어떻게 관리할 것인가다.

노동정책은 기존의 논쟁이 더 이상 현실에 맞지 않는 이유를 보여준다. 정년을 60세 이상으로 연장해야 한다는 주장은 실제 문제를 반영한다. 많은 근로자들이 국민연금 수급 자격을 갖추기 수 년 전에 일자리를 떠나고 있다. 한편 기업들은 한국의 연공급 임금제 하에서 직원들을 계속 고용하면 노동비용이 급격히 증가하면서 신규 채용 유인이 떨어진다고 주장한다. 하지만 이 문제를 고령 근로자와 청년 구직자 간의 경쟁으로 보는 것은 증상을 원인으로 착각하는 것이다. 더 근본적인 제약은 생산성보다 근속연수를 더 보상하는 임금체계다. 임금제도를 개혁하지 않고 정년을 연장하면 채용 유인과 경쟁력을 모두 약화시킬 수 있다. 더 유연한 퇴직 후 재고용과 직무급 및 성과급으로의 점진적 전환이 더욱 지속 가능한 타협안이 될 수 있다.

같은 논리가 연금과 복지에도 적용된다. 한국의 노년 부양비는 29.9까지 올라 대략 3.3명의 경제활동 가능 인구가 한 명의 노인을 부양하고 있다. 고령화지수는 200을 넘어 어린이 1명당 노인이 2명 이상이다. 조세 기반의 확대 속도가 더딘 가운데서도 연금, 의료, 장기요양에 대한 공공 지출은 필연적으로 증가할 것이다. 근로자의 기여금 인상이나 혜택 조정 같은 점진적 조정은 재정 부담을 미룰 수는 있지만 근본적인 불균형을 해결할 수는 없다. 한국은 궁극적으로 국민연금, 기초연금, 직역연금 체계의 통합을 강화하고 선거일정이 아닌 인구통계 변화에 대응하는 자동조정 메커니즘을 도입해야 한다.

이민과 지역 발전도 같은 장기적 관점이 필요하다. 외국인 주민이 이제 한국 인구의 4.1%를 차지하고 있으며 이 중 89.3%가 경제활동 가능 연령대다. 제조업, 농업, 요양서비스에 대한 그들의 기여는 이미 상당하다. 하지만 임시 노동 프로그램으로는 축소되는 국내 노동력을 대체할 수 없다. 한국은 영구적으로 정착하려는 고숙련 전문가들을 더 적극적으로 확보해야 한다. 또 다른 중요한 이슈는 수도권에 인구의 50.9%가 집중되면서 주택 공급 압박이 심화되고 지역 경제가 공동화되고 있다는 점이다. 강력한 지역 산업 기반이 중앙정부의 재정 이전 확대보다 더 중요해질 것이다.

경제 적응은 노동시장을 넘어선다. 이제 서울 가구의 40% 이상이 1인 가구인데, 대가족을 위해 설계된 주택 모델이 점점 구식이 되고 있다. 시장과 정책 입안자 모두 소비 패턴, 주택 수요, 노인 돌봄의 변화에 적응해야 하며, 동시에 인공지능 및 기타 생산성 향상 기술에 대한 투자는 축소되는 노동력을 보충하는 데 도움이 될 것이다.

인구통계적 기준은 흔히 이정표로 묘사된다. 실제로는 제도들이 그것을 지탱하고 있는 사회를 따라가지 못하기 시작하는 지점을 나타낸다. 한국은 임시방편 대책이 아닌 구조적 적응을 훨씬 더 많이 요구하는 시대에 진입했다. 한국이 번영과 사회적 응집력을 유지할 수 있을지는 노동시장, 연금제도, 그리고 광범위한 경제 구조가 변화하는 인구와 함께 얼마나 성공적으로 진화하는가에 달려 있을 것이다.

editorials.title: Demographic threshold
editorials.body: ‘Superaged’ South Korea must redesign labor, welfare, growth for an irreversibly older society South Korea did not become old in a single year. Yet every society eventually reaches the point where demographic forecasts stop describing the future and begin describing the present. That moment arrived this week. Official 2025 census data, released Tuesday by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, showed that people aged 65 or older made up 20.7 percent of the population, formally placing Korea among the world's superaged societies. At the same time, the working-age population fell to 69.2 percent, slipping below the 70 percent mark for the first time since comparable records began in 2015. Those numbers are less remarkable for crossing arbitrary thresholds than for confirming something more consequential. The country is no longer approaching a demographic transition; it has completed one. The challenge is therefore no longer how to restore the population structure, but how to manage a permanently older and slower-growing society without sacrificing productivity or social cohesion. Labor policy illustrates why old debates no longer fit today's realities. Calls to extend the mandatory retirement age beyond 60 reflect a genuine problem: Many workers leave their jobs several years before becoming eligible for the national pension. Businesses, meanwhile, argue that retaining employees under Korea's seniority-based wage system would sharply increase labor costs while discouraging new hiring. Treating the issue as a contest between older workers and younger job seekers, however, mistakes the symptom for the cause. The deeper constraint is a compensation system that rewards tenure more than productivity. Without reforming wages, extending retirement could weaken hiring incentives and competitiveness alike. More flexible post-retirement reemployment, combined with a gradual shift toward job-based and performance-based pay, would offer a more sustainable compromise. The same logic applies to pensions and welfare. Korea's old-age dependency ratio has climbed to 29.9, meaning roughly 3.3 working-age adults support one senior. The aging index has surpassed 200, leaving more than two older people for every child. Public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care will inevitably rise even as the tax base expands more slowly. Incremental adjustments, such as asking workers to contribute more or modifying benefits, may delay fiscal strain but cannot resolve the underlying imbalance. Korea ultimately needs better integration of its national, basic and occupational pension systems, together with automatic adjustment mechanisms that respond to demographic change instead of electoral calendars. Immigration and regional development require the same long-term perspective. Foreign residents now account for 4.1 percent of Korea's population, and 89.3 percent of them are of working age. Their contribution to manufacturing, agriculture and care services is already substantial. Yet temporary labor programs cannot substitute for a shrinking domestic workforce. Korea should compete more aggressively for highly skilled professionals willing to settle permanently. Another critical issue is the continued concentration of 50.9 percent of the population in the Seoul metropolitan area, deepening housing pressures while hollowing out regional economies. Stronger local industrial bases will matter more than larger central government transfers. Economic adaptation extends beyond labor markets. More than 40 percent of Seoul households now consist of a single person, making housing models designed for larger families increasingly outdated. Markets and policymakers alike must adjust to changing patterns of consumption, housing demand and elder care, while investment in AI and other productivity-enhancing technologies helps compensate for a smaller workforce. Demographic thresholds are often described as milestones. In reality, they mark the point when institutions begin to lag behind the society they were built to serve. Korea has entered an era that demands fewer temporary fixes and far more structural adaptation. Whether the country remains prosperous and cohesive will hinge on how successfully its labor market, pension system and broader economic architecture evolve alongside its changing population. Five consecutive days of temperatures above 40 degrees have made life-threatening heat waves commonplace.
Urgent reform of response systems to the level of social disaster is needed.

Life-threatening extreme heat has settled over South Jeolla and Gwangju and 17 districts in South Gyeongsangnam-do.
